title: Flash Airlines 604
summary: The Boeing 737-300 crashed into the Red Sea three minutes after takeoff from Sharm El Sheikh. After takeoff, the autopilot abruptly disconnected and the aircraft entered a steep right bank that increased to 111 degrees where it stalled. The NTSB and BEA concluded the pilot suffered spatial disorientation and the copilot was unwilling to challenge the more experienced captain.
probable_cause: The NTSB and BEA concluded that the pilot suffered spatial disorientation and the copilot was unwilling to challenge his more experienced superior. Egyptian authorities disagreed, instead blaming mechanical issues.

factors.evidence: The autopilot abruptly disconnected at which point the aircraft entered a right bank of 40 degrees.
The NTSB and BEA concluded that the pilot suffered spatial disorientation.
The copilot was unwilling to challenge his more experienced superior.
Both officers were insufficiently trained.
The aircraft entered a stall and crashed into the Red Sea at 04:45 EGY, just three minutes after takeoff.

events.text: The aircraft departed and made a left turn to intercept the airport's VOR system, and the autopilot was then engaged; Captain Khedr made an unintelligible exclamation and the autopilot abruptly disconnected.
The aircraft entered a right bank of 40 degrees and the bank angle increased further.
First Officer al-Shaafei called out 'overbank,' indicating that the aircraft's bank was becoming dangerous.
The aircraft entered a stall and crashed into the Red Sea at 04:45 EGY, just three minutes after takeoff.

title: Uzbekistan Airways 1154
summary: Flight 1154 collided with radar station while landing at Tashkent in fog. Aircraft descended below glideslope and was 30-40 meters high at runway threshold when should have been lower. Right wing struck beacon/light stanchion tearing wing, hit concrete wall, flipped and exploded.
probable_cause: Early indications suggested bad weather caused accident. Aircraft descended below glideslope without proper landing configuration.

factors.evidence: Airport shrouded in fog limiting visibility to 1300 meters
Aircraft descended below glideslope 12.5 km from airport
Crew became aware too late running out of runway at 30-40 meters
Aircraft not in landing configuration at runway threshold
Right wing struck radio beacon or approach light, aircraft flipped and exploded

events.text: Flight 1154 cleared to land at Tashkent in full darkness and fog
At 12.5 km from airport, increased rate of descent bringing below glideslope
Maintained level flight until nearer airport, still 30-40 meters high at runway
Right wing struck radio beacon or stanchion, left wing struck wall, aircraft flipped and exploded

title: Kish Air 7170
summary: Flight 7170 lost control and crashed on approach to Sharjah after an incorrect control input deployed the thrust reversers in flight. The captain unexpectedly asked the first officer to conduct the approach; the first officer became nervous and allowed the aircraft to fly high. When the captain attempted to reduce altitude by pulling the thrust lever ground range selector, he inadvertently deployed reverse pitch propellers in mid-air. The aircraft entered a steep dive and rolled heavily to the left before striking the ground. Forty-three of the 46 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: Captain suddenly asked first officer to conduct approach, causing nervousness that led to aircraft being high on approach; captain then accidentally deployed reverse pitch propellers in mid-air while attempting to decrease altitude, causing loss of control.

factors.evidence: captain suddenly asked the first officer to conduct the approach, taking the unprepared first officer by surprise, causing him to be nervous
first officer was surprised by the captain's decision and stated he was not confident enough on his ability to conduct the approach
captain accidentally caused the throttles to enter the reverse range by pulling the thrust lever's ground range selector
propeller speed jumped causing a noisy sound and reverser had been deployed in mid-air
aircraft pitched down and rolled to the left at more than 30 degrees, entered steep left bank dive and spiral
aircraft crossed a road and exploded on impact, bursting into flames; fire rapidly spread and engulfed fuselage

events.text: Shortly before descent, Captain Hosseini asked First Officer Panahian to switch roles and become pilot flying
Captain Hosseini pulled thrust lever ground range selector to decrease altitude
Propeller speed jumped and caused loud noisy sound; aircraft pitched down and rolled left over 30 degrees
Captain realized reverser deployed in mid-air and instructed to move lever fully forward
Aircraft continued in heavy left bank until it struck ground 2.6 nmi from end of runway, exploding on impact

title: Rico Linhas Aéreas 4815

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos

location.name: Amazon rainforest, 64 nm from Manaus, Brazil

summary: Rico Linhas Aéreas Flight 4815, an Embraer EMB 120ER Brasilia, departed Tefé Airport at 17:30 local time on approach to Manaus, Brazil. At 18:34, the aircraft was given its last radar heading guidance while maintaining 2,000 feet; the crew confirmed these instructions. Less than 30 seconds later at 18:35:03, the aircraft impacted the equatorial rainforest at an altitude of 550 feet at over 250 knots with wings level. Both pilots were highly experienced with thousands of flight hours on type. All 33 passengers and crew were killed. The cockpit voice recorder was recovered and analyzed, but the exact cause could not be established from available evidence.
probable_cause: The investigation determined the aircraft was flown below assigned altitude during descent, resulting in terrain impact in the dense Amazon rainforest. The exact cause could not be established from available evidence.

factors.evidence: At 18:35:03 the aircraft impacted the equatorial forest at 550 feet while having been instructed to maintain 2,000 feet.
The crew allowed the aircraft to descend below assigned altitude without calling out or correcting the altitude deviation.
The aircraft crashed into equatorial rainforest at 550 feet altitude at over 250 knots with wings level.

events.text: Aircraft departed Tefé Airport at 17:30 AMT en route to Manaus at 64 nm distance.
At 18:26, aircraft was cleared to descend to 8,000 feet from cruise altitude.
Subsequently cleared to descend to 2,000 feet for radar vectoring separation.
At 18:35:03, aircraft impacted equatorial rainforest at 550 feet altitude, wings level, over 250 knots airspeed; CVR recording ended upon impact.

notes: Exact cause could not be established from available evidence

title: 2004 Russian aircraft bombings
summary: On the night of 24 August 2004, two domestic Russian passenger flights crashed after explosive devices detonated on board, killing all 89 occupants. Volga-AviaExpress Flight 1303 (Tu-134, 43 aboard) crashed first in Tula Oblast, followed minutes later by Siberia Airlines Flight 1047 (Tu-154, 46 aboard) in Rostov Oblast. Both flight data recorders showed high-energy events at cruise altitude indicating structural failure from explosions. Subsequent investigations concluded two Chechen female suicide bombers were responsible.
probable_cause: Explosive devices detonated in passenger cabins of both aircraft at cruise altitude.

factors.evidence: Two Chechen female suicide bombers were responsible for the bombings; both flights carried explosive devices that detonated during cruise.
Flight 1303 FDR indicated high-energy event at seat row 19; Flight 1047 FDR showed similar event at seat row 25. Both events triggered explosive decompression and loss of cabin pressure.
The blast resulted in rapid decompression, damage to elevator and rudder controls, substantial loss of electrical power, and severe damage to fuselage and tail components.
Both aircraft lost control following the explosions; Flight 1047 crew were caught completely off guard with no evidence they were aware of explosive detonation before impact.

events.text: Flight 1303 departed Domodedovo International Airport at 22:30 on 24 August 2004 bound for Volgograd.
Flight 1303 communication lost while flying over Tula Oblast, 180 km south of Moscow; explosive device detonated.
Flight 1047 departed Domodedovo International Airport at 21:35 bound for Sochi.
Flight 1047 broadcast Emergency Locator Transmitter signal while flying over Rostov Oblast; aircraft disappeared from radar screens.
Debris of Flight 1047 found 9 km from work settlement of Gluboky in Rostov Oblast; both aircraft completely destroyed at cruise altitude.

title: MK Airlines 1602
summary: Flight 1602 took off from Halifax with incorrect takeoff data due to crew reusing a lighter weight (240,000 kg instead of 353,000 kg) from a previous flight at Bradley. This led to wrong V speeds and thrust settings. During takeoff rotation, the aircraft experienced tailstrikes but continued airborne. It then struck an earthen berm 300 m beyond the runway and broke apart in flames. Fatigue from duty time violations and unfamiliarity with weight calculation procedures contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: The crew calculated incorrect takeoff weight, resulting in wrong V speeds and thrust settings that led to inappropriate rotation and tailstrikes during takeoff. The company's lack of duty time rules contributed to crew fatigue, which increased the likelihood of such errors.

factors.evidence: incorrect V speed calculation, as the result of the crew re-using a lighter take-off weight of 240000 kg from the aircraft's previous take-off at Bradley, instead of the correct weight of 353000 kg
crew's unfamiliarity with the use of the Boeing Laptop Tool, which calculated the proper power requirement
no regulations or company rules governing maximum duty periods for loadmasters and ground engineers resulting in increased potential for fatigue-induced errors
the aircraft began to rotate and tailstrike occurred at the 8000 ft mark, and a second tailstrike took place with 420 ft of runway remaining
The lower aft fuselage then struck an earthen berm supporting an instrument landing system (ILS) localizer antenna 300 m beyond the end of the runway
breaking into pieces and bursting into flames when it struck the ground

events.text: Flight 1602 taxied to Runway 24 and the takeoff roll was commenced
When the aircraft reached 130 knots, the control column was moved aft to 8.4 degrees to initiate rotation
The aircraft began to rotate and tailstrike occurred at the 8000 ft mark
With 420 ft remaining, a second tailstrike took place
The aircraft became airborne approximately 670 ft beyond the paved surface
The lower aft fuselage then struck an earthen berm supporting an instrument landing system (ILS) localizer antenna 300 m beyond the end of the runway
The plane then headed forwards in a straight line for another 1200 ft, breaking into pieces and bursting into flames

title: Pinnacle Airlines 3701
summary: On a repositioning ferry flight, two Pinnacle Airlines pilots intentionally climbed a Bombardier CRJ200 to 41,000 ft, the aircraft's maximum operating altitude. Without maintaining adequate airspeed for the high altitude, the aircraft stalled, both engines flamed out, and the crew failed to execute proper recovery procedures. The aircraft crashed short of Jefferson City Memorial Airport with total loss of life.
probable_cause: Pilot-induced loss of control in flight resulting from intentional climb to maximum altitude without maintaining safe airspeed, followed by inadequate response to dual engine failure and stall. Contributing was aggressive maneuvering and deviation from standard operating procedures.

factors.evidence: Crew climbed to 41,000 ft, maximum operating altitude, where safe speed margins are minimal
Due to low energy state of the aircraft, it subsequently stalled and both engines flamed out
Crew aggressively maneuvered the aircraft with pitch-up to 22 degrees nose-up and rudder inputs during climb
Aircraft stalled due to low airspeed at high altitude
Due to interrupted airflow, both engines flamed out
Aircraft departed controlled flight in upset and crashed in residential area

events.text: Aircraft departed Little Rock with flight plan indicating cruising altitude of 33,000 ft
Autopilot engaged while climbing through 14,000 ft
Autopilot disengaged, crew made aggressive pitch-up maneuver with nose up 17 degrees and 2.3 Gs load
At 24,600 ft, crew conducted pitch-up maneuver with 10 degrees nose-up attitude and 1.87 Gs
Aircraft stalled at 41,000 ft maximum altitude without adequate airspeed for the altitude
Both engines flamed out from interrupted airflow following stall
Captain declared emergency to ATC after aircraft upset; crew managed to recover from upset at 34,000 ft
Aircraft crashed in residential area short of Jefferson City Memorial Airport

notes: Detailed flight data and CVR transcripts provide clear evidence of crew actions and aircraft state
Investigation findings extensively documented by NTSB
Sequence of aggressive maneuvering leading to stall well-established

title: Corporate Airlines 5966
summary: Corporate Airlines Flight 5966, a Jetstream 32 twin-engine turboprop, crashed on approach to Kirksville Regional Airport near Pettis Township, Missouri, on 19 October 2004. Captain Kim Sasse and First Officer Jonathan Palmer were conducting a non-precision instrument approach at night in instrument meteorological conditions. The aircraft descended below the minimum descent altitude into a region without guaranteed obstacle clearance, struck trees, and crashed. Both pilots were killed along with 11 of 13 passengers.
probable_cause: Pilots' failure to follow established procedures and properly conduct non-precision instrument approach at night in IMC, specifically their descent below minimum descent altitude before required visual cues were available, and their failure to maintain established division of duties between flying and monitoring pilots. Contributing factors: crew fatigue from 14-hour duty day and failure to make standard callouts.

factors.evidence: Pilots descended below minimum descent altitude before required visual cues were available, continuing unmoderated until aircraft struck trees
Both pilots were looking outside cockpit for visual cues rather than monitoring instruments; first officer did not challenge captain to maintain instrument scan
First officer failed to challenge captain and maintain professional monitoring duties; failure to establish professional demeanor during flight
Pilots had worked 14-hour duty day including six flights, degrading performance despite regulations last updated in 1964
Pilots failed to follow established procedures and make standard callouts during non-precision approach
Night instrument meteorological conditions with no visual references to airport or terrain
Aircraft struck trees during descent on approach and crashed near Kirksville

events.text: Flight 5966 departed St. Louis Lambert on evening of 19 October 2004 for Kirksville; crew had already completed six flights on 14-hour duty day
Aircraft cleared for non-precision instrument approach to Kirksville in night IMC conditions
Captain Sasse began looking outside cockpit for visual cues to runway location
Captian continued descent below MDA; first officer did not challenge or call attention to descent rate
Aircraft struck trees and crashed during continued unmoderated descent below minimum descent altitude

notes: NTSB analysis of cockpit voice recorder noted captain should have been monitoring instruments rather than searching outside for visual references; report included recommendation that FAA revise fatigue regulations

title: China Eastern Airlines 5210
summary: Two minutes after takeoff from Baotou, the Bombardier CRJ200ER fell from the sky and crashed into a lake in Nanhai Park adjacent to the airport. The aircraft had not been deiced by ground crew while parked on the tarmac overnight. Ice accumulation on the wings caused the aircraft to lose lift, resulting in immediate loss of control. The crash killed all 53 people on board and 2 park employees on the ground. Investigation confirmed the de-icing omission as the cause.
probable_cause: The aircraft had not been deiced by the ground crew while it was parked on the tarmac. Ice accumulation on the wings caused the aircraft to lose its lift and crash immediately after takeoff.

factors.evidence: ice accumulation on the wings caused the plane to lose its lift
the plane had not been deiced by the ground crew while it was parked on the tarmac

title: Lion Air 538
summary: Lion Air Flight 538, an MD-82 landing at Surakarta in heavy rain during dusk, overran the rain-soaked runway and impacted a concrete localizer antenna base. The investigation concluded that hydroplaning was the primary cause, aggravated by wind shear. The aircraft's braking system was not at optimum level, and a faulty thrust reverser was identified as one of the causes.
probable_cause: The plane's braking system was not at its optimum level. This condition was aggravated by weather conditions during the accident. A faulty thrust reverser was identified as one of the causes of the crash, as the pilot did not put the throttle into flight idle, which caused the spoiler to retract.
